The question this page answers

Where can people and firms actually reach financial services — and where is the map still blank?

Access: where services can be reached is only partly mapped

Parts of the access picture are documented: the provider lists of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden), its reported total of 1,651 point-of-sale (POS) terminals in June 2026 within its reporting scope, dated status decisions, and a 2016–2019 study showing e-money accounts concentrated in cities. The evidence does not yet establish, consistently across Yemen, which access points are operating at a particular place and date.

How numbers are presented

Every consequential number stays attached to its unit, scope, time and limitation. Evidence measured at different times is never presented as if it described the same moment.

What this does not establish

What a roster or infrastructure count cannot establish

A licence or roster entry does not prove current operation at every named location. A system-level count of terminals or service points does not establish where people can reach a service. Missing geography is unknown, not zero, and spatial overlap with electricity, connectivity, population or conflict does not by itself establish causality.

What we still do not know

Why this resource does not show a complete map now

A missing location record is not evidence that no service exists. Where operation cannot be verified, this resource shows the location as not observed or not currently evidenced. It does not turn an unobserved point into zero, or a licence, branch name or historical provider study into current operating presence.

03Evidence

What official lists and payment reports can show

Official rosters and decisions can establish listing, licensing or a dated status event. Payment reports issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) can establish system totals within that bank’s reporting scope for specified dates; how far that scope covers each area of Yemen is not established. These are useful pieces of the access picture, but they are not a verified, geocoded network of operating service points.

04Evidence

Lists show who is registered, not where services operate

Official lists document a substantial exchange and remittance provider presence relevant to the access question. The 2026 roster of the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 100 exchange companies, 231 individual exchange establishments and 111 remittance agents — three source categories, not a deduplicated count of firms — and the CBY-Aden list of licensed banks, as checked on 3 October 2026, names 26 banks. Listing or licensing is not operation. The 2026 suspension, withdrawal or closure decisions are separate status events: they are dated January–September 2026, some were issued before the roster and some after it, and the roster’s own issue date is not stated. Separately, the results framework of the World Bank-financed Financial Market Infrastructure and Inclusion Project (FMIIP) sets a January 2025 baseline of 817 financial access points against a 2030 target of 1,021, under a project definition that the evidence base does not document. None of these figures shows where services operate or how far people are from them.

05Analysis

Infrastructure can expand without telling us who can reach it

POS terminals reported by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) rose from 561 in March 2025 to 1,651 in June 2026, within that bank’s reporting scope. This establishes a change in the reported terminal stock. It does not show where every terminal is located, how many merchants or unique users it represents, whether the terminals are active, or how evenly access is distributed.

Another view of the evidence
06Measurement

What a reliable national access atlas would require

For each service point, a reliable access atlas would require — subject to safety and rights — the permitted location or geographic level, channel type, operator, operating status, last verification date, available services, and any restriction on publication or spatial precision. Population, travel time, connectivity and conflict/access constraints could then be added as separate dated layers.

Analysis

Historical provider evidence shows concentration, not a map of access after 2019

A five-provider study covering 2016–2019 reports that e-money accounts/users were concentrated in cities at an average 93.8%, while women represented about 13% on average. It reports 807,919 e-money accounts in December 2019 and an average dormant/inactive share of 23%. These are historical observations for the providers the study covered. They are useful for showing why account counts cannot be read as active people or current geographic access; they are not national prevalence or a present-day access map.

System context

Where access sits in the wider system

Access sits between the presence of providers or infrastructure and actual use. Understanding it requires evidence on provider authority and operating status, reachable geography, channel and service type, followed separately by evidence on whether people or firms actually use the service and the quality they experience.

Evidence periodGlobal Findex fieldwork 2022–2023 · point-of-sale (POS) counts March 2025 – June 2026 · project baseline January 2025, target 2030
When the unit changes, the story changes
People, accounts, subscribers, terminals and transactions all describe parts of Yemen’s financial system. They are not interchangeable measures of financial inclusion, and a target or a trend is only as sound as the unit it keeps.

What measurement would change the decision?

Measurement priorityP0 · Providers / Geography
A register of active financial access points
Current official rosters establish selected listing, licensing and event states, but do not provide a complete, geocoded register of active branches, agents, merchants and other service points.
Evidence needed: An authoritative or jointly documented register of individual access points recording type, active status, date, location and services, plus population denominators and road-network data that allow coverage and travel distance or time to be calculated.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would distinguish listing and licensing from operation and observed access before any access or opportunity map is interpreted.
Open this measurement priority
Measurement priorityP0 · Reforms / Payments / Quality
Reform transmission and service quality
Recent evidence documents rules, institutions, projects, procurement and selected infrastructure activity, but the chain to access, use, quality and outcomes is incomplete.
Evidence needed: Reform-specific operational and user-side evidence tied to the same implementation timeline, from go-live through coverage, reliability, cost and outcome.
Decision it would strengthen: This evidence would show the furthest evidenced state of each reform and the next unmeasured result without treating missing evidence as failure.

When was it measured or observed?The official 2026 roster (issue date not stated); 2026 enforcement decisions are separate evidence.
The official 2026 exchange and remittance roster can be counted; whether providers operate now is a separate question
The official 2026 roster of exchange and remittance providers issued by the Central Bank of Yemen – Aden (CBY-Aden) lists 100 exchange companies, 231 individual exchange establishments and 111 remittance agents. These are roster entries counted by the roster's own classes: the three class totals are not a count of unique providers, nor a verified count of providers operating now. Because the roster does not state its issue date, CBY-Aden's 2026 decisions (dated January to September 2026) suspending or withdrawing the licences of named entities, or closing their premises, would have to be matched with the roster entity by entity, since a decision may or may not already be reflected in it; that matching has not been done.
Who or what does it apply to? Source-listed exchange companies, individual exchange establishments and remittance agents; entries are counted separately by the three classes used in the official roster.
